title: The Lantern
logline: A neighbourhood spends weeks building a great Vesak lantern of bamboo and paper, lights it for a few nights, then takes it apart.

object.note: Object 1 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: From a procession's fire to a neighbourhood's paper lights: something built with great care, seen for a few nights, then taken apart.

thread_out.thread: As the lantern comes down, the first thing found beneath the names is wanting: the colours of lantern paper give way to cloth unfolded bolt after bolt, and something wanted badly.

lesson.in_simple_terms: A great Vesak lantern is bamboo, paper and light held in one shape for a few nights, and when it is taken apart the name 'lantern' goes with it. The texts look at everything, even a person, in this way, and say that wherever something seems lovely, wanting quietly begins.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: වෙසක් කූඩුවක් යනු බට, කඩදාසි සහ එළිය දින කිහිපයකට එක් හැඩයකට සකස් කළ දෙයක් පමණක් වුවත්, ප්‍රිය යැයි හැඟෙන තැනම තණ්හාව නිහඬව හටගන්නා බව ධර්මය උගන්වයි.
lesson.the_teaching: The texts gather everything conditioned into five heaps (khandha), each a collection of many passing moments of one kind, and explain that the division exists to take apart the habit of saying 'I' and 'mine' about each of them. A lantern, like a boat or a cloth, is a collective and shape concept (paññatti) that lasts only while its parts are arranged. The compendium then places all of this under four truths, and names craving (taṇhā), which takes the aggregates as something good and pleasant and clings to them, as the real cause of suffering.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film follows the lantern from bamboo cut and tied, through paper and colour, to the first lighting and the crowd's wonder, and then to the bare frame being taken down the next week. The viewer feels the care poured into something everyone knows will not last, and notices, in the faces lit by it, the first stirring of wanting it to stay.

key_terms.en: craving: for sense pleasure, for existence, for non-existence

lesson.caution: This does not mean the lantern, the effort or the joy is worthless, or that one should stop wanting anything; the texts name a particular clinging thirst, not every wish, and taking things apart is meant to loosen grasping, not to make the world colder.
lesson.builds_on: The ring of fire existed only while the flame kept moving; the lantern exists only while its parts are held together, and its taking-apart brings the series to the first thing found beneath the names: wanting.
